div.head: Editorial Introduction
div.p: This digital edition presents Ella C. Evanson’s “Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda,” a typescript narrative preserved in the Ella Evanson Scrapbooks held by University of Washington Libraries Special Collections. Produced in Seattle in the early 1940s, the text emerges from the wartime classroom culture of Washington School[18], where Evanson taught students from diverse racial backgrounds. The story centers on a Chinese student, Ming Chin, and his classmates’ efforts to raise funds for a baby giant panda. At the same time, its references to China, Japan, war, and classroom conflict place the story within the broader context of World War II and the racial tensions that shaped Asian American life on the West Coast.

Our edition treats “Ming Chin and the Baby Giant Panda” not only as a children’s story, but also as a social and archival artifact. The narrative preserves traces of classroom life, wartime feeling, racial language, and the ways global conflict entered the everyday world of students. As Yoon K. Pak argues in Wherever I Go, I Will Always Be a Loyal American, Seattle’s Japanese American schoolchildren experienced a painful contradiction between democratic citizenship education and the racial exclusion authorized by Executive Order 9066[17]. Although Evanson’s story focuses on a Chinese student, its classroom setting and its reference to anti-Japanese language make it important for understanding the racialized atmosphere of Seattle schools during the war.

Our editorial approach is primarily diplomatic. We preserve original spelling, punctuation, capitalization, grammar, and historically charged language rather than modernizing or sanitizing the document. We use TEI markup to identify people, places, historical references, and key terms, while editorial notes provide historical and archival context. This apparatus is designed to help readers understand the story as both a literary text and a record of wartime student experience and local Asian American history in Seattle.

div.head: MING CHIN AND THE BABY GIANT PANDA
div.p: James Smith strutted up to the front of the schoolroom and said, "Miss Brown, may I make an announcement?"
"Yes, certainly, James."
"As treasurer of the Baby Giant Panda Fund[1], I wish to report that the last penny is in and now we can pay for our baby giant panda."
The noisy applause that followed was offset by the report of Miss Brown[2], "I am sorry to tell you that on account of the war the panda cannot yet be brought over from China."
Miss Brown's announcement was met by stunned silence, then Sylvia voiced her resentment, "And after we worked so hard to raise the money! It's a gyp[3]!"
Toji[4], appropriately said, "Those Japs[5] have no business in China."
All the children were sad but Ming Chin seemed saddest.

"I wonder why Ming is so sad," said James as he watched the tall boy hurrying down the street to Yesler School[6] a few days later. Each morning Ming Chin arrived breathless barely beating the tardy bell deadline.
"Bet I'd be plenty happy if I could do such good work," said the black-faced Abe[7].
"He makes me feel like a chiseler," James continued, "studying every minute. He works in his brother's laundry on Pike Street, too. His father is in China."
"Isn't that enough to make him sad? Work in school every minute and work after school?" Abe's sympathy was evident.
Miss Brown, realizing Ming Chin's loneliness, found a way to unlock his tense lips.
"Ming, I'd like to hear about your home in China. How long since you left? What does your father do?"
The class suddenly stopped. They had keen ears for stories.
A look of happiness changed the handsome face of the fourteen-year-old boy, and though he spoke timidly in a low voice, not one of the forty interested listeners missed a word.
"Two year were pass since I leave China. My father was professor of zoology in school in Hong Kong."
"I get it," said James. "That's why you're always Studying."
But Abe said, "Why didn't your father come when you came?"
"My father stay because my grandfather very sick. My grandfather die last year. Hong Kong is lost.[8] If my father not die, money all gone. War take all money. No money for ticket to America."
"Anyway, how can your father come here? I thought the United States wouldn't let any more Chinese enter."[9] James was remembering his history.

"He is student and he will go to school here. Chinese students can stay in United States."[10] Then his face revealed the mystery of his sadness and his audience saw it instantly. "No money for ticket." But he added with determination. "My brother and I work hard to get money for ticket."
Miss Brown suddenly thought, perhaps this is the answer to an important question, and she went to the records to look up Ming Chin's father.
The next morning Ming again closed the schoolroom door behind him as the last bell was ringing. James was waiting.
"Ming, what I've tried to find out is where they have sent all the civilians that got away from HongKong before the seige began. I wonder where your father is."
Ming, disconsolate, though not yet hopeless, spoke. "He go to China, far from coast, maybe, but now more far from America."
"Well, consoled Abe, "at least he is safer than in Hong Kong. Who knows, he may be on his way to Seattle by this time!"
Day after day the speculation continued, and each day Ming's conclusion was, "Now my father farther from America. Never come, maybe."
China, instead of a remote spot on the globe became to the class a real place absorbing all interest. They were especially fascinated by the zigzag airplane views of the Burma Road[11].
"Can you feature that? Gosh, what a roller coaster that would make!" was Abe's comment.
"Roller coaster is rignt. Did you see in the movies how the trucks got through with the supplies to China before the fall of Rangoon[12]?"
Miss Brown, recalling the children's panda stranded in China asked, "Ming, does your father know a good deal about wild animals? Do you think he would be willing to play nurse to a baby giant panda?"

Ming fairly jumped with surprise. The giant panda was one of his father's favorite subjects. "A giant panda! Many years past my father go to Shanghai to see giant panda American lady found.[13] It was baby," and Ming cradled his hands to indicate the size.
"Giant pandas are very scarce," said Toji.

James was very alert to the trend of the conversation. "I read about that. They found it in the mountains of western China and flew with it to Shanghai, then went by boat to San Francisco, and on to New York. What do you mean, Miss Brown, have they really found a way to bring our baby giant panda to us?"

"Yes, I have a friend connected with the zoo in Woodland Park[14] who has for months been trying to bring over the baby panda which they have secured for us, but due to war re-strictions they are forbidden to take it out of China."
"Well, pandas grow like Jack's beanstalk."
"That's what's worrying the zoo officials."
"How big is it?"
"It was only a few weeks old when they found it nearly three months ago. It probably weigns fifteen pounds now. The bigger it grows the more difficult it is to transport."
Many of the children felt that there was more to the story but the class bell rang.
"What happened to the panda? a disappointed chorus shouted. "Can't you tell us now?"
"It's too long a story. Besides, the bell rang, and you must be in your next class on time. I'll tell you tomorrow."

The next morning the weekly assembly took place when Miss Brown's class should have met, and there was no opportunity to go on with the story. The subject was, however, immediately resumed the following day.
"Miss Brown, why did you ask Ming all those questions about his father and the panda?"

"Now I can tell the secret." Everyone relaxed in his seat. "As I told you yesterday, the Woodland Park Zoo is very anxious about our panda. The curator, as the keeper is called, was delighted when it was suggested that Ming's father bring the baby panda to this country."

Ming was astounded. He could not follow the swift ways of Americans. Abe was puzzled. "But there's a war over there. How's he going to get here? Boats aren't safe even if they were still running between China and the United States."
James had the answer, "The clipper![15] I read that pandas are good travelers even in the air, and on water, too."

Miss Brown settled the question. "You are both right. Our government has arranged the transportation of the panda and his keeper by land, water, and air. It believes the panda is of sufficient value to warrant the expense even in war time. The brave boys who were our own American Volunteers, the Flying Tigers[16], have been given the responsibility of carrying the baby panda to some place on the coast."
James, impatient to near tue rest, asked, "Where do they go from there, and how?"

"They plan to start the long fourteen thousand mile journey by way of New Zealand. Transports bring materials for China and on their return trip they will bring the precious panda. It's fortunate he is a good traveler."
The class sat speechless but not for long. The confusion of chattering voices gave way to one persistent question, "Does it mean that Ming's father is really coming?"
The silence was as sudden and as effective as a rest in a stormy musical number. Ming's feet moved as if to brace himself.
Miss Brown answered slowly, "Yes. Uncertain conditions make it impossible to predict when, but we have the assur-ance that Ming's father will arrive some time."
"Oh gee, I can't wait, can you, Ming?"
"My father come soon maybe, "Ming replied almost unbelieving.
"We do know, continued Miss Brown, "that they are already on the way."
The harsh ringing of the buzzer interrupted the story with the signal that there was a telephone call for Miss Brown. As she left the room, they sank down as if exhausted by a difficult problem.
"I thought so all along. I knew he'd get here," exulted Abe.
Everyone was talking at once and they failed to notice the return of Miss Brown until she stood in their midst.
"Looks like more mystery! Now what happened? Oh do hurry, Miss Brown, what were you going to say?"
"A big surprise, You could never guess! That telephone message changed what I was going to say. Ming's father and the baby giant panda arrived in Seattle safely and unexpectedly."
"Then why did they say that about the long journey by water?" The children hated to give up the idea of the Flying Tigers having a hand.

"Well, it seems there was room on a plane returning with army and navy officers. Naturally, they couldn't broadcast that news. And of course, it was wise to get the panda here as soon as possible. I'm as surprised as you. I thought they were just starting the long ocean voyage."

The amazed children, relieved after days of anxiety, cheered uproariously. Abe's voice was the first to be heard above the din. "Let's go to the zoo, Miss Brown. Can't we all go? We want to see the giant baby panda and Ming's father, too."
Suddenly, the realization that Ming's troubles were over and their own desires completely satisfied, they turned earnest eyes toward Ming who confidently declared, "Now my fatner come."

list.item: 1. The Baby Giant Panda Fund reflects the popular fascination with giant pandas in the United States in the late 1930s and early 1940s, when live pandas from China became major zoo attractions and objects of public fundraising. In the story, the children’s fundraising project connects classroom life in Seattle to trans-Pacific cultural exchange and wartime disruption. Croke 2005.

2. Miss Brown appears to be based on Ella C. Evanson, the teacher and writer associated with the classroom materials preserved in the Ella Evanson Scrapbooks. Evanson’s role as both educator and collector makes the text important as a literary artifact and as a record of classroom culture. Evanson Archive.

3. The term “gyp” is preserved here as part of the historical text. It is now recognized as an offensive term linked to stereotypes about Romani people. Its presence in the text reflects the casual circulation of racialized language in the period and should be read critically.

4. The name Toji may be connected to Tooji, the student author of “My Ambition,” another text associated with Evanson’s classroom archive. This connection suggests that Evanson may have drawn on student names, voices, or classroom experience in shaping her fiction. Pak 2002.

5. This anti-Japanese slur is preserved because it appears in the source text and reflects wartime racial hostility after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Its presence shows how global conflict and anti-Japanese sentiment entered children’s classroom speech and social dynamics. Warren 1999.

6. Yesler School refers to a Seattle public school context near the city’s Central District and International District neighborhoods. Its mention helps locate the story within a local geography of multiethnic schooling.
7. The phrase “black-faced Abe” is preserved as part of the source text. It reflects the racial language of the historical document and should be read critically rather than as a neutral description.
8. Hong Kong fell to Japanese forces in December 1941, shortly after the attack on Pearl Harbor. This wartime context shapes Ming Chin’s fear that his father may be unable to reach the United States.

9. James’s comment refers broadly to the history of Chinese exclusion in the United States, especially immigration restrictions that limited Chinese entry before the repeal of the Chinese Exclusion laws during World War II.
10. The text distinguishes Chinese students from other Chinese migrants, suggesting the special status of students within immigration regimes and educational exchange.

11. The Burma Road was a crucial wartime supply route used to transport materials to China during the Second Sino-Japanese War and World War II. In the story, the children’s fascination with the Burma Road shows how wartime geography entered the classroom imagination.

12. Rangoon, now Yangon, was an important port and transport hub in Burma. Its fall in 1942 disrupted Allied supply routes to China and intensified the wartime difficulty of moving people, goods, and animals across Asia.

13. The “American lady” likely refers to Ruth Harkness, who brought the first live giant panda to the United States in the 1930s. Her expedition helped produce American popular fascination with pandas and made the animal a symbol of adventure, rarity, and Sino-American connection. Croke 2005.

14. Woodland Park refers to Woodland Park Zoo in Seattle. In the story, the zoo connects local children’s fundraising to trans-Pacific wartime movement and to the broader public culture of animal display.

15. “The clipper” refers to long-distance flying boats associated with transoceanic air travel, such as Pan American’s clipper service. The reference links the story’s panda rescue plot to the modern technologies of air transport.

16. The Flying Tigers were the American Volunteer Group that fought in China before the United States formally entered World War II. In the story, their mention connects the children’s panda project to wartime aviation and the Sino-American alliance.

17. Executive Order 9066, signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 19 February 1942, authorized the Secretary of War and designated military commanders to establish military areas from which “any or all persons” might be excluded. Although no specific group was named, it was enforced primarily against people of Japanese ancestry, resulting in the incarceration of approximately 120,000 individuals, the majority of whom were American citizens. National Archives.

18. George Washington School, referred to in this collection as Washington School, was a public junior high school in Seattle’s Central District where Ella Evanson taught seventh and eighth grade from 1928 until her retirement in 1956. The school was known for its commitment to democratic ideals and racial tolerance, serving students from Japanese American, Chinese American, Jewish, African American, and white families. Evanson Archive.
